hook: America's 'most innovative company' was hiding its losses in fake partnerships.
summary: Enron began in 1985 as a Houston gas-pipeline company and reinvented itself as a high-flying energy trader that Wall Street adored. Executives used aggressive accounting and off-balance-sheet partnerships to hide debt and invent profits, and when the truth came out in 2001 the company collapsed into bankruptcy, wiping out employees' savings and taking its auditor Arthur Andersen down with it. Lesson: if you can't explain in plain words how your company makes money, something is wrong.
learn: How mark-to-market accounting let Enron book profits it had not earned
How off-balance-sheet partnerships hid debt from investors
Why employees lost their savings when the stock collapsed

hook: A 158-year-old bank bet big on home loans and died in one weekend.
summary: Lehman Brothers began as a small store in Montgomery, Alabama, run by German immigrant brothers, and grew into one of Wall Street's biggest investment banks. In the 2000s it borrowed heavily to pile into real-estate and mortgage bets; when the housing market cracked, no buyer or rescue came, and Lehman filed the largest bankruptcy in US history on 15 September 2008, setting off a global panic. Lesson: borrowed money magnifies a bad bet until a single weekend can end 150 years of work.

hook: WeWork rented offices, called itself a tech company, and hit a $47B price tag.
summary: WeWork leased office buildings, turned them into trendy shared workspaces and rented out desks by the month. Fuelled by billions from SoftBank it was valued at $47 billion, but its 2019 IPO filing revealed huge losses and conflicts of interest, the IPO was pulled, Neumann was pushed out, and WeWork filed for bankruptcy in 2023. Lesson: a great story can raise money, but the numbers on each desk still have to work.

hook: The world's biggest phone maker sold its phone business 6 years after the iPhone.
summary: Nokia started in 1865 as a Finnish paper mill and became the world's largest mobile-phone maker by the late 1990s. It saw smartphones coming, but its software was clunky and fear and internal politics slowed decisions; after Apple and Android took over, it bet on Microsoft's Windows Phone and then sold its handset business to Microsoft in 2013. Nokia survived by reinventing itself as a telecom-network company, proof that the hardest part of any shift is changing your own culture.

hook: Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975, then let others win the digital age.
summary: George Eastman made photography easy for everyone ('You press the button, we do the rest') and Kodak grew rich selling film. In 1975 its own engineer Steve Sasson built the first digital camera, but film was so profitable that Kodak moved slowly into digital, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012. Lesson: protecting today's profits can stop you from building the future.

hook: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million. It said no.
summary: Blockbuster opened in 1985 and became the world's biggest video-rental chain, earning a big slice of its profit from late fees that customers hated. In 2000 it turned down a chance to buy a tiny Netflix for $50 million, moved too late into DVDs-by-mail and streaming, and filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Lesson: if customers resent the way you make money, a competitor will build a business on removing that pain.

summary: Research In Motion was founded in Waterloo, Canada in 1984, and its BlackBerry, with secure email and a physical keyboard, became the must-have phone for businesses and governments. When the iPhone and Android moved phones toward touchscreens and apps, BlackBerry's leaders underestimated the change, and its market share collapsed within a few years. Lesson: what your loyal customers want today may not be what the market wants tomorrow.

hook: Yahoo turned down Microsoft's $44.6B offer. Years later it sold for about $4.5B.
summary: Two Stanford PhD students started Yahoo in 1994 as a list of their favourite websites, and it became the front door of the early internet. It kept changing what it wanted to be, passed on chances to buy Google, rejected Microsoft's $44.6 billion offer in 2008 and churned through CEOs, until Verizon bought its core business in 2017 for about $4.5 billion. Lesson: a company that doesn't know what it is gets beaten by companies that do.

summary: Hollywood veteran Jeffrey Katzenberg and former eBay CEO Meg Whitman launched Quibi in April 2020 with $1.75 billion and star-studded short shows made only for phones. It launched just as COVID lockdowns kept people at home, didn't let users easily share clips, and competed with free YouTube and TikTok; it announced it was shutting down about six months later. Lesson: money and famous names can't replace testing whether people actually want your product.

In 2017 Bloomberg showed the packs could be squeezed by hand almost as well, the story went viral, and Juicero shut down a few months later. Lesson: brilliant engineering is worthless if it doesn't beat the simple alternative.

summary: Pets.com was one of the most hyped startups of the 1999–2000 internet boom, selling pet food and supplies online with a famous sock-puppet mascot. Shipping heavy, cheap bags of food often cost more than customers paid, and when the dot-com bubble burst it shut down in November 2000, the same year it went public. Lesson: growth means nothing if each sale loses money; CEO Julie Wainwright later used those lessons to build The RealReal.

hook: Toys 'R' Us didn't die from Amazon alone. It died carrying billions in buyout debt.
summary: Charles Lazarus turned a baby-furniture shop into Toys 'R' Us, the giant toy superstore loved by generations of kids. In 2005 private-equity firms bought it in a leveraged buyout that loaded it with about $5 billion of debt, leaving little money to fix stores or fight Walmart and Amazon; it filed for bankruptcy in 2017 and closed its US stores in 2018. Lesson: debt can quietly strangle a business that still has loyal customers.

hook: Sears was the Amazon of 1900: one catalog that sold everything. Then it fell behind.
summary: Richard Sears started selling watches by mail in 1886, and the Sears catalog let farm families order almost anything, making it America's biggest retailer for decades. It was slow to respond to Walmart, discount chains and online shopping, and after a 2005 merger with Kmart under hedge-fund owner Eddie Lampert it split into competing internal units and sold off assets, filing for bankruptcy in 2018. Lesson: being the original disruptor doesn't protect you from the next one.

hook: GE was once America's most valuable company. Then it was split into three.
summary: Born from Thomas Edison's electric companies, General Electric became America's most admired conglomerate, and under Jack Welch it was the most valuable US company by 2000, with much of its profit coming from its finance arm, GE Capital. The 2008 crisis showed how risky GE Capital was, costly bets such as a big push into power turbines went wrong, and GE spent years selling businesses before splitting into three companies by 2024. Lesson: smooth-looking earnings can hide big risks, and complexity is not the same as strength.

hook: VW's 'clean diesel' cars had secret software that cheated emissions tests.
summary: Volkswagen sold its diesel cars as 'clean diesel' while racing to become the world's biggest carmaker. In 2014 researchers at West Virginia University found the cars polluted far more on real roads than in lab tests, and in 2015 VW admitted about 11 million cars worldwide carried software that detected tests and switched on full pollution controls only then. Fines, buybacks and settlements cost it more than $30 billion and several executives faced criminal charges; the lesson is that a culture that rewards hitting targets at any cost will eventually cheat.

hook: A former NASDAQ chairman ran the biggest Ponzi scheme in history for decades.
summary: Bernie Madoff founded his trading firm in 1960 and became a respected Wall Street figure, even serving as chairman of the NASDAQ. For decades his investment business paid steady 'returns' that were really other investors' money; analyst Harry Markopolos warned regulators for years, but the scheme only collapsed in December 2008 when clients asked for their money back. Madoff pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 150 years in prison; the lesson is that returns too smooth to be true usually are.

founders: John Meriwether, with Myron Scholes, Robert Merton and others
hook: Two Nobel winners helped run this hedge fund. It nearly broke Wall Street in 1998.
summary: LTCM was founded in 1994 by star bond trader John Meriwether with a team that included Nobel-winning economists Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, and it made spectacular early returns from tiny price gaps, using enormous amounts of borrowed money. In 1998 Russia's debt default sent markets haywire, the gaps widened instead of closing, and the fund lost most of its capital in months, so the New York Fed organised a $3.6 billion rescue by banks. Lesson: clever models fail when you ignore rare events, and heavy borrowing leaves no time to recover.

hook: Nikola's truck in the promo video wasn't driving. It was rolling downhill.
summary: Trevor Milton founded Nikola in 2014 promising zero-emission hydrogen and electric trucks, and after going public in 2020 it was briefly worth more than Ford. Short-seller Hindenburg Research then showed that a promotional video of a truck 'in motion' had been filmed rolling down a hill; Milton resigned, was convicted of fraud in 2022 for misleading investors (he was pardoned in 2025), and Nikola filed for bankruptcy in 2025. Lesson: hype can buy time, but sooner or later the product has to work.

summary: Wirecard started in 1999 processing online payments and grew into one of Germany's most valuable companies. Financial Times reporter Dan McCrum spent years exposing accounting problems while German authorities investigated the journalists instead; in June 2020 Wirecard admitted that €1.9 billion of cash probably did not exist and collapsed into insolvency. Former CEO Markus Braun went on trial in Munich in 2022 and denies wrongdoing; the lesson is that honest audits and a free press matter more than a soaring share price.

hook: FTX customers' money was secretly funnelled to its sister trading firm.

founders: Aaron Burr (The Manhattan Company, 1799); J. Pierpont Morgan (J.P. Morgan & Co., 1871)
hook: Jamie Dimon was fired from Citigroup. He went on to build America's biggest bank.
summary: JPMorgan Chase is the product of more than 200 years of bank mergers, from Aaron Burr's Manhattan Company to J. Pierpont Morgan's famous firm. With partner Charlie Munger he used the cash from insurance businesses to buy great companies and hold stocks for decades, turning Berkshire into one of the world's most valuable companies. Buffett handed the CEO role to Greg Abel at the end of 2025; the lesson is that patience, honesty and compounding beat cleverness.

hook: Ray Dalio started Bridgewater in his apartment and built the world's biggest hedge fund.

Lesson: write down how you make decisions, test them against reality, and be honest when they fail.

hook: A codebreaker-turned-math professor built Wall Street's most successful fund.
summary: Jim Simons was a prize-winning mathematician and former Cold War codebreaker who left academia in 1978 to trade markets. Instead of hiring traders, Renaissance hired mathematicians, physicists and computer scientists to find patterns in data, and its Medallion Fund produced returns widely considered the best in investing history. Lesson: hire brilliant people from outside your industry and let evidence overrule gut feeling.

founders: Larry Fink and seven partners, including Robert Kapito and Susan Wagner
hook: Larry Fink lost $100M at First Boston, then built the world's biggest money manager.
summary: Larry Fink co-founded BlackRock in 1988 after his bond desk at First Boston lost about $100 million on a wrong interest-rate bet, and he built the new firm around managing risk, including its Aladdin software. BlackRock grew into the world's largest asset manager, helped by its iShares index funds, and in 2025 it entered India's mutual-fund market through JioBlackRock, a joint venture with Mukesh Ambani's Jio Financial Services. Lesson: a painful failure can become the founding idea of your next company.

hook: Jack Bogle was fired, then built a fund company owned by its own customers.
summary: After being fired as head of Wellington Management in 1974, Jack Bogle founded Vanguard in 1975 with an unusual structure: the company is owned by its funds, and so by its investors. In 1976 he launched the first index fund for ordinary investors, mocked as 'Bogle's Folly', and low-cost index investing went on to reshape the whole industry. Lesson: aligning your business with your customers' interests can be the ultimate advantage.

hook: Chuck Schwab bet that ordinary people wanted cheap stock trades, not salesmen.
summary: Charles Schwab started a small investment firm in 1971 and, when US rules on fixed trading commissions ended in 1975, turned it into a discount broker that let regular people trade cheaply without paying for a salesman. He sold the firm to Bank of America in 1983, bought it back in 1987, and kept cutting costs until Schwab became one of America's biggest brokerages. Lesson: when a rule change opens a door, the founder who walks through it on the customer's side can build an empire.

hook: Ken Griffin traded from his Harvard dorm with a satellite dish. Then he built Citadel.
summary: Ken Griffin started trading from his Harvard dorm room, famously putting a satellite dish on the roof to get live prices, and founded Citadel in Chicago in 1990. It survived a near-death moment in 2008 when its main funds lost about half their value, and grew into one of the world's most profitable hedge funds alongside Citadel Securities, a giant market maker. Lesson: obsessive focus on talent, technology and risk control can turn a dorm-room experiment into a powerhouse.

hook: Sequoia backed Apple, Atari and Cisco by asking one question: how big is the market?
summary: Don Valentine, a former chip salesman at Fairchild and National Semiconductor, founded Sequoia Capital in 1972 and backed Atari, Apple and Cisco early. His rule was to 'target big markets': a huge market can rescue an ordinary team, but not the other way round, and Sequoia went on to back Google, YouTube, WhatsApp and Nvidia. Lesson: choose a problem big enough that winning is worth it.

founders: Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris & Trevor Blackwell
hook: Y Combinator began as a summer experiment funding eight student startups.
summary: In 2005 Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell ran a 'Summer Founders Program', giving small cheques and advice to a batch of student startups that included Reddit. The batch model worked so well that YC became the world's best-known startup accelerator, backing Airbnb, Stripe, Dropbox and thousands more. Lesson: start small, run an experiment, and let the results tell you whether to scale.

hook: Two Irish brothers made online payments take minutes instead of weeks.
summary: Brothers Patrick and John Collison, who grew up in rural Ireland, started Stripe in 2010 because accepting payments online was slow and painful for developers. Their simple tools let a startup start charging customers with a few lines of code, and Stripe grew into one of the world's most valuable private companies, processing payments for millions of businesses. Lesson: obsess over the user's experience in a boring but essential problem.

founders: Max Levchin, Peter Thiel, Luke Nosek & Ken Howery (Confinity); merged with Elon Musk’s X.com
hook: PayPal nearly died from fraud. Fighting fraud became its secret weapon.
summary: PayPal began as Confinity in 1998, merged with Elon Musk's X.com in 2000, and made sending money by email a hit with eBay sellers. Criminals quickly stole millions, and co-founder Max Levchin's team built pioneering fraud-detection systems that turned the problem into an advantage; eBay bought PayPal for $1.5 billion in 2002, and its alumni went on to found or fund YouTube, LinkedIn, Yelp, Palantir and more. Lesson: the hardest problem in your business can become your moat.

founders: A group of US banks (Interbank Card Association)
hook: A Pune-born CEO, Ajay Banga, pushed Mastercard deep into digital payments.
summary: Mastercard began in 1966 when a group of US banks formed the Interbank Card Association to compete with BankAmericard (later Visa). It was owned by its member banks until its 2006 IPO, and under Pune-born IIM Ahmedabad graduate Ajay Banga, CEO from 2010 to 2020, it pushed hard into digital payments and financial inclusion. Lesson: a network business wins by making every new user more valuable to all the others.

hook: American Express started by delivering parcels. Then it invented the traveler's cheque.
summary: American Express was founded in 1850 as a freight and express-delivery company, moved into money orders and, in 1891, invented the traveler's cheque. Its charge card, launched in 1958, became a status symbol, and the company survived shocks such as the 1963 'salad oil scandal' and the 9/11 attacks beside its New York headquarters, when CEO Ken Chenault led it through the crisis. Lesson: a trusted brand can reinvent its products many times over.

hook: Masa Son turned $20M in Alibaba into a fortune, then lost billions on WeWork.
summary: Masayoshi Son, a Korean-Japanese entrepreneur who studied at UC Berkeley, founded SoftBank in 1981 as a software distributor and turned it into a giant technology investor. His $20 million bet on Alibaba in 2000 became worth tens of billions, but his $100 billion Vision Fund also poured money into WeWork and other startups that crashed. Lesson: bold bets create huge wins and huge losses, so understand what you are paying for, not just the vision.
